L783: Reencryption Simulatability.
L784: While HRA is a strictly stronger security notion than CPA, we now show that if
L785: a CPA secure proxy reencryption scheme has an additional property we call
L786: reencryption simulatability, then it must also be HRA secure. Very roughly,
L787: reencryption simulatability means that ciphertexts resulting from computing
L788: ReEnc(rki→j, cti) can be simulated without knowledge of the sender’s secret key
L789: ski (but with knowledge of the plaintext message m and the recipient’s secret
L790: key skj). Note that ReEnc uses rki→j which is a function of ski.
L791: Reencryption simulatability allows an algorithm with access to the CPA or-
L792: acles to eﬃciently implement the honest reencryption oracle. For intuition, con-
L793: sider the following approach to reducing HRA security to CPA security. Suppose
L794: 9 [31] separate the computation of θ∗
L795: i from Bob’s public key, but this is only a matter
L796: of presentation.
L797: 18
L798: there existed an adversary Ahra violating the HRA security of a scheme; the re-
L799: duction plays the roles of both the CPA adversary and the challenger in the HRA
L800: security game, and attempts to violate CPA security. To succeed, the reduction
L801: must be able to answer honest reencryption queries from uncorrupted keys to
L802: corrupted keys. Though the reduction knows the messages being reencrypted,
L803: it does not know the appropriate reencryption key. However, if it could indis-
L804: tinguishably simulate these reencryptions then it could indeed leverage Ahra to
L805: violate CPA security.
L806: We emphasize that the goal of Deﬁnition 7 is to capture a large swath of
L807: possible schemes while still enabling very simple proofs of simulatability (and
L808: thus of HRA security for existing CPA secure schemes). It is not intended to be
L809: the only avenue for proving HRA security of new or existing constructions. Reen-
L810: cryption simulatability is not necessary for HRA security of proxy reencryption.
L811: In particular, analogous versions of Theorem 5 hold with computational simu-
L812: latability guarantees, but are more complicated [15, Foonote 7 and Appendix
L813: A].
L814: Deﬁnition 7 (Reencryption Simulatability). A proxy reencryption scheme
L815: PRE is reencryption simulatable if there exists a probabilistic, polynomial-time
L816: algorithm ReEncSim such that with high probability over aux, for all m ∈M:
L817: (ReEncSim(aux), aux) ≈s (ReEnc(rka→b, cta), aux),
L818: where ≈s denotes statistical indistinguishability, and cta and aux are sampled
L819: according to
L820: pp ←Setup(1λ),
L821: (pka, ska) ←KeyGen(pp),
L822: (pkb, skb) ←KeyGen(pp),
L823: rka→b ←ReKeyGen(ska, pkb),
L824: cta ←Enc(pka, m),
L825: aux = (pp, pka, pkb, skb, cta, m).
L826: A special case of the above is when ReEncSim(aux) = Enc(pkb, m) simply com-
L827: putes a fresh encryption of the message. That is, if reencrypted ciphertexts are
L828: distributed like fresh ciphertexts, then the scheme is reencryption simulatable.
L829: Theorem 5. Let PRE be an CPA secure, reencryption simulatable, proxy reen-
L830: cryption scheme. Then PRE is HRA secure.

L837: Acpa runs Ahra and simulates the HRA security game (if Ahra does not follow
L838: the speciﬁcation of the HRA security game, Acpa simply aborts). To answer
L839: 19
L840: oracle calls by Ahra to any oracle other than OReEnc, Acpa simply passes the calls
L841: and answers unaltered to the corresponding CPA oracles.
L842: To answer oracle calls to OReEnc between two uncorrupted keys or two cor-
L843: rupted keys, Acpa uses the corresponding reencryption key. On the other hand,
L844: for calls to OReEnc from an uncorrupted key to a corrupted key, Acpa simulates
L845: the reencryption using ReEncSim. This is possible because Acpa knows the un-
L846: derlying m (along with the other information in aux).
L847: Reencryption simulatability implies that the views of Ahra in the real security
L848: game (using the real OReEnc) and the simulated security game (using ReEncSim)
L849: are statistically close. Acpa wins the CPA security game if and only if Ahra wins
L850: in the simulated HRA game described above.
L851: 5.3
L852: Fully Homomorphic Encryption and Proxy Reencryption
L853: There is an intimate connection between FHE and proxy reencryption: a suﬃ-
L854: ciently powerful somewhat homomorphic encryption scheme implies CPA secure
L855: proxy reencryption, which can be used to “bootstrap” the scheme to achieve
L856: fully homomorphic encryption [19]. For the relevant FHE deﬁnitions, see [19,
L857: Section 2].
L858: Let FHE = (SetupFHE, KeyGenFHE, EncFHE, DecFHE, EvalFHE) be an FHE scheme.
L859: Proxy reencryption can be constructed as follows (compare to the Trivial Scheme):
L860: KeyGenPRE, EncPRE and DecPRE are identical to their FHE counterparts.
L861: ReKeyGenPRE(ski, pkj) = EncFHE(pkj, ski)∥pkj. The reencryption key rki→j is
L862: an encryption under pkj of ski, along with the target public key pkj.
L863: ReEncPRE(rki→j, cti): Let cti→j ←EncFHE(pkj, cti). Homomorphically compute
L864: the FHE decryption function DecFHE(ski, cti) using the corresponding cipher-
L865: texts rki→j and cti→j (under pkj). Namely, ctj = EvalFHE(pkj, DecFHE, rki→j, cti→j).
L866: The correctness of the FHE implies the correctness of the resulting proxy reen-
L867: cryption:
L868: DecPRE(skj, ctj) = DecFHE(skj, ctj) = DecFHE(ski, cti) = DecPRE(ski, cti).
L869: Furthermore, the proxy reencryption scheme is CPA secure.
L870: To demonstrate that the construction might not be HRA secure, consider
L871: the following fully homomorphic encryption scheme FHE′ constructed from any
L872: existing scheme FHE. The only modiﬁcation made in FHE′ is to EvalFHE′:
L873: EvalFHE′(pkj, C, ct1, ct2) := EvalFHE(pkj, C, ct1, ct2)∥ct1.
L874: Note that FHE′ does not violate FHE compactness if ct1 (in the proxy reencryp-
L875: tion construction, rki→j) is always of some size bounded by a polynomial in the
L876: security parameter of the FHE scheme; this suﬃces for our purpose. Instanti-
L877: ating the proxy reencryption construction with FHE′ essentially results in the
L878: Concatenation Scheme, which is not HRA secure.
L879: 20
L880: Circuit Privacy. An FHE scheme is circuit private if ciphertexts resulting
L881: from FHE evaluations are statistically indistinguishable from fresh ciphertexts
L882: [19]. Namely, if for any circuit C and any ciphertexts ct1,. . . ,ctt:
L883: EncFHE(pk, C(ct1, . . . , ctt)) ≈s EvalFHE(pk, C, ct1, . . . , ctt).
L884: In [19], an FHE scheme without circuit privacy is modiﬁed to be circuit private
L885: by rerandomizing the ciphertexts resulting from EvalFHE.
L886: While our proxy reencryption construction above is not in general HRA se-
L887: cure, it is easy to see that if the underlying FHE is circuit private, then the
L888: proxy reencryption is reencryption simulatable (Deﬁnition 7). By Theorem 5,
L889: the resulting scheme is therefore HRA secure.
